notes.h: Identifying a trend through the elements of design
notes.b: A trend is recognised by the features it repeats across many garments and outfits. The elements of design (colour, shape, line, proportion, pattern and texture) give you the words to describe those features, and the examples below are only examples, because the trend shown in an exam may be any current one.
points: Colour: bright, fluorescent or tonal colour schemes, colour panelling and monochrome outfits make a trend easy to spot from a distance.
Shape and silhouette: oversized or boxy shapes, high-waisted trousers, and tailored coats or capes. Cropped tops are another example of a current shape.
Line: exaggerated vertical lines add height, horizontal lines widen and shorten the look, and diagonal lines give contrast and movement. This is why a trend can be described through its lines.
Proportion: for example a short jacket worn over a long dress, or a deep cropped top with wide trousers.
Pattern: geometric prints and bold retro statements. Retro patterns are old designs revived by designers, so name the pattern and say it is a revival.
Texture: shiny finishes reflect light, while matt fabrics absorb it. Embroidery, sequins, beads and distressed or frayed surfaces add surface interest.
Accessories: belts, large bags, statement jewellery and hats, which can carry a trend on their own.

Seasonal examples are examples of their year, not fixed lists: summer 2024 gave light leggings, loose T-shirts, crochet knits, denim jackets, cut-outs, cargo trousers and oversized jackets. Teenage trends gave ripped denim, bomber jackets and chunky jewellery. Casual wear showed neon and panelled colour and geometric prints.
notes.tip: Name and describe the trend first, in terms of colour, shape, line and fabric, and say why it suits the wearer. Then judge it. Male and female trends both count, so evaluate one of each or choose one.

notes.b: Trends do not appear by accident. Several forces decide which colours, garments and styles become popular, and exams ask you to outline or evaluate these influences.
points: Social media spreads a fashion image internationally within hours, and repeated exposure can turn a colour, garment or vintage look into a trend. This is why trends also increase sales.
Influencers and bloggers display outfits and styling videos, give samples and feedback, and their endorsements can encourage or discourage a purchase.
Celebrities, musicians and athletes are photographed in specific designers' clothes, and fans copy their style. Music and dance styles, sports and world events also shape what people wear.
Designers and fashion houses define the season's direction through seasonal collections and fashion weeks. Ready-to-wear (mass-produced) clothing then copies the runway looks.

Environmental concern has created demand for sustainable or circular fashion (clothing kept in use for as long as possible). This favours durable natural or recycled materials, repair and upcycling, and fast fashion is criticised for waste.
Trends are also shaped by travel and by culture, including global and ethnic styles from other countries that become popular at home.
Past decades return: retro and vintage styles and bold retro patterns are revived by designers and high street brands.
notes.tip: Evaluating social media means covering speed of spread, influencers' samples and reviews, the effect on sales, and encouraging or discouraging purchases. For a question on three factors, pick clearly different ones, such as celebrities and influencers, designers, environmental issues, music and dance, travel and culture, or world events.

notes.b: Athleisure (also called leisure wear) is sportswear styling worn for everyday life, not sportswear for playing sport. It has become a major trend because it puts comfort first.
points: Typical items include leggings or joggers, hoodies, zipped jackets and trainers, worn for work, school and leisure.
Stretch, breathable and easy-care fabrics give comfort and freedom of movement, and they wash easily, which suits busy everyday use.
Its strengths are comfort, versatility, durability, affordability and adaptability to many occasions. It is casual and trendy and is promoted by influencers.
Athleisure can support activity and posture and a healthy active lifestyle, since clothing that is comfortable to wear makes it easier to exercise and move.
It works as a wardrobe staple (a basic item worn again and again) when the pieces are neutral in colour and can be combined with smarter items.
Its weaknesses are that it can look too informal for some workplaces and occasions, and that tight leggings and tops do not suit every body shape.
Another weakness is that it may encourage a casual dress code to become the default in everyday life.
notes.tip: Athleisure is examined as a wardrobe staple, as the emergence of leisure wear, and as the suitability of an outfit shown. Give a strength and a weakness, and relate both to the wearer and the occasion.

notes.b: Buying older or second-hand clothes has moved from a bargain habit to a fashion statement. The two terms are different, and both are examined.
points: Vintage clothing is older clothing from a past era, often a previous decade. Pre-loved clothing is any second-hand clothing, so all vintage is pre-loved but not all pre-loved is vintage.
Both are bought in charity shops, vintage or second-hand shops, online marketplaces and swaps.
Pre-loved clothing extends the life of garments already made, which reduces the demand for new production. This is why it is linked to sustainability and the reaction to fast fashion.

Reasons for its popularity: it is cheaper than new, it gives a unique, individual look because fewer people wear the same piece, and influencers and celebrities promote it. The economic climate also encourages it.
Distressed looks, such as frayed edges, grated patches and bleached areas, take inspiration from the vintage punk look, along with studs, sequins and embroidery.

Retro statements, such as bold patterns and bright colours from earlier decades, are revived by designers and high street brands. They are eye-catching because they stand out from plain everyday wear.
Upcycling changes an old garment into a new one, for example by adding patches, embroidery or appliqué (fabric shapes sewn on), dyeing, shortening, or customising denim with studs.

To restyle a garment to follow a trend, add belts or embellishment, alter the hem or trouser length, add layers or shoulder pads, crop or deconstruct a jacket, distress or recolour jeans, or change the buttons, patches or linings.
notes.tip: For popularity questions, cover cost, individuality, sustainability and the reaction to fast fashion. A pattern, influences and accessories part may also be asked, so link retro patterns, sustainability and upcycling, and accessories that draw attention and tie the outfit together.

notes.h: Accessories as part of a trend
notes.b: Accessories are the items added to an outfit rather than the main garments. They are often the quickest way to show a trend.
points: Examples include belts, bags, scarves, hats, gloves, jewellery, sunglasses, footwear, ties, cufflinks and pocket squares.
Accessories complete an outfit and create a focal point (the place the eye goes first), drawing attention to a feature of the look. A belt, for example, shows off the waist.
They add colour and contrast, and they tie an outfit together by repeating a colour from another garment. A colourful scarf brightens a plain outfit.
Accessories can change the formality of a basic outfit, for example a scarf or hat that makes a plain outfit look smart or casual. They also help balance colour and proportion.
A vintage look can be created with items such as retro sunglasses, large brooches and patterned scarves.
Footwear contributes to the overall look, complements the outfit and can create a focal point.
Accessories are often the cheapest way to follow a trend, as one item can update or modernise an existing outfit.
notes.tip: When asked to suggest one accessory, name it and give a reason in terms of emphasis, colour coordination, formality or completing the look. A reason is what earns the marks, not the name alone.

notes.b: A critical evaluation weighs the advantages and disadvantages of a trend rather than simply describing it. Describe the trend first, then judge it under the headings the question gives.
points: Advantages: a trend can express identity, create employment in the fashion sector and bring new ideas to design.
Disadvantages: fast fashion encourages frequent buying, leading to waste and to garments of low quality that wear out quickly.
Cost: following trends can be expensive, and garments may date quickly once a trend passes.
Comfort and function: a trend should be judged on whether the garment is comfortable and suits the wearer's activity.
Suitability: a trend may not flatter every body shape, so a critical evaluation considers who it suits and who it does not, and the occasion it is worn for.
Other headings the exam may give include colour, pattern, line, shape, proportion, texture, accessories, aesthetic appeal and influences.
notes.tip: Always give at least one strength and one weakness, using the headings in the question, such as colour and pattern, line and shape, or accessories.

notes.h: Sketching an outfit that reflects a trend
notes.b: Elective questions ask you to sketch and describe an outfit built around one current trend, so you need to show the trend and explain your choices.
points: Diagram: draw a front view of the outfit (add a back view if needed) and label the design features, such as line, shape, proportion and harmony. Give the colour and fabric, and say which trend it follows and why.

Fabric reasoning: choose for a reason, such as absorbent, breathable, stretch, easy-care or shape-retaining. Cotton-elastane jersey suits fitted tops because it stretches, and polyester/cotton suits durable jackets and joggers.
Aesthetic appeal: explain how colour, line, balance and emphasis work together, and how the outfit suits the wearer and the occasion.
notes.tip: The sketch is a labelled fashion drawing, with a description of the trend and its suitability. Labelled features and a reason for the fabric are what the question asks for.

keyTerms.definition: The overall outline or shape of a garment when it is worn.
Clothing that combines sportswear, such as leggings, joggers and hoodies, with everyday dress.
A person with a large social media following whose choices of clothing and products are copied by others.
Second-hand clothing from an earlier period, often valued for its style and age.
Turning an old or unwanted garment into a new one with a higher value, for example by adding patches or embroidery.
Inexpensive, quickly produced clothing that follows trends closely and is designed to be replaced frequently.
A finish that makes new garments look worn, through frayed edges, grated patches or bleaching.
An approach to clothing in which garments are designed to be repaired, reused or recycled to keep materials in use.

factCards.definition: Bleaching and frayed or distressed edges.

questions.prompt: Describe two ways that social media influences current fashion trends.
questions.model: Social media spreads a fashion image internationally within hours, so a colour, garment or vintage look can become a trend quickly. Influencers and celebrities display outfits, styling videos and shopping links, so followers can copy the look immediately and buy the items shown.

questions.prompt: Critically evaluate a current fashion trend of your choice, referring to its use of colour, line or shape, and its comfort and function.
questions.model: Name the trend, such as athleisure, and describe its key features. Colour: neutral or monochrome colour schemes give a sleek, coordinated look, and bright colours add interest. Line and shape: relaxed, oversized or stretch silhouettes allow movement and suit many body shapes, but a very loose shape can make a short wearer look shorter. Comfort and function: stretch, breathable fabrics allow free movement and absorb perspiration, and the garment can be worn for work, school or exercise. Evaluation: the trend is versatile and affordable, but it can look too informal for some workplaces, and fast production of such garments creates waste and wears out quickly. A conclusion weighs the advantages against the disadvantages and states whether the trend is suitable for the wearer.
